title: MVC (Model-View-Controller) Pattern
oneLiner: Splits an application into Model (data), View (display), and Controller (input handling) so each can change independently.

hero.name: The Triad
hero.catchphrase: Three roles, one flow: data, display, and decisions, each in their lane.
hero.power: Separates data, presentation, and input-handling into three distinct roles, so a UI redesign never touches business logic.
hero.weakness: As apps grow, the Controller becomes a magnet for logic that doesn't cleanly belong to Model or View — the classic 'fat controller' problem.
hero.origin: The Triad appeared after a blog engine's single `PostPage.php` file mixed SQL queries, HTML markup, and form-handling logic in one 800-line file that nobody wanted to touch.

story.problem: `PostPage.php` mixes SQL queries, HTML markup, and form-submission handling in one 800-line file. Changing how a post displays risks breaking how posts get saved.
story.solution: The Triad splits it three ways: `Post` (Model) holds data and business rules, `PostView` (View) only renders markup, and `PostController` (Controller) handles input and coordinates the other two.
story.result: A redesign only touches PostView. A new validation rule only touches Post. Each role can change without risking the others.

before: Data, display, and input logic tangled in one file
A display change risks breaking data logic
Impossible to test business logic without rendering HTML
after: Data, display, and input logic live in three separate roles
A display change only touches the View
Business logic in the Model is testable with no HTML involved

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: An 800-line file mixes SQL, HTML, and form-handling logic with no clear boundaries between them.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I changed the post layout and somehow broke how comments get saved. Everything in this file touches everything else.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Triad appears as three distinct figures, each holding one clear responsibility.
panels.speaker: The Triad
panels.dialogue: Stop mixing three jobs into one file. Data goes in the Model. Display goes in the View. Input handling goes in the Controller.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Post (Model) holds data and rules. PostView renders markup. PostController handles form submissions and coordinates both.
panels.speaker: The Triad
panels.dialogue: The Controller takes input, asks the Model to update, then tells the View to re-render. Each role only knows its own job.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: A redesign of the post layout touches only PostView. Comment-saving logic is untouched.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I redesigned the whole layout and didn't come close to the comment-saving logic. They're finally separate.

useWhen: An application has clear data, presentation, and input-handling concerns that would benefit from separation.
Multiple views might need to display the same underlying data differently.
You want business logic (Model) to be testable independently of any UI framework.
avoidWhen: The application is trivially small, with no meaningful separation to gain.
Your framework already provides a more specific, better-fitting pattern (like MVVM's data binding for rich client UIs).
You'd be forcing MVC's structure onto something that doesn't naturally have three distinct concerns (like a pure CLI script).
commonMistakes: Letting the Controller accumulate business logic that belongs in the Model — the classic 'fat controller' anti-pattern.
Letting the View reach directly into the database or business logic, bypassing the Model/Controller separation entirely.
Treating MVC as one-size-fits-all when a variant (MVP, MVVM) actually fits the UI technology better.
Conflating 'MVC' across wildly different frameworks — server-side MVC (Rails, Django) and client-side MVC (older Backbone-style) differ significantly in practice.
explanation.realWorldExample: Ruby on Rails, Django, ASP.NET MVC, and Spring MVC are all explicitly built around this pattern for server-rendered web applications.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from MVP or MVVM?

conversation.speaker: The Triad
conversation.message: We're a family. In classic MVC, the View can talk somewhat directly to the Model. MVP makes the View fully passive, mediated entirely by a Presenter. MVVM goes further, binding the View to a ViewModel's observable state automatically.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's the most common way I misuse you?

conversation.speaker: The Triad
conversation.message: Fat controllers. The moment your Controller starts validating business rules or querying the database directly instead of delegating to the Model, you've broken the separation I exist to provide.

codeBattle.scenario: Your server-rendered web app has HTML generation, SQL queries, and form-validation logic all mixed together in single route handler files, and every new feature makes the tangle worse.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Triad separates data (Model), rendering (View), and input handling (Controller) into distinct, independently changeable roles, exactly matching this tangled route-handler problem.

quiz.question: What are the three roles in MVC?
quiz.explanation: These three roles, each with a distinct responsibility, are exactly what the pattern's name spells out.

quiz.question: What is the 'fat controller' anti-pattern?
options: The Controller accumulates business logic that should live in the Model
The Controller has too many unit tests
The Controller is too small to do anything useful
The Controller directly renders HTML instead of delegating to the View
quiz.answer: The Controller accumulates business logic that should live in the Model
quiz.explanation: This is the most common way MVC's separation of concerns erodes over time in real codebases.

quiz.question: What benefit does separating the Model provide?
options: Business logic can be tested independently of any UI or HTML rendering
It makes the application run faster in every case
It removes the need for a database
quiz.answer: Business logic can be tested independently of any UI or HTML rendering
quiz.explanation: A Model with no UI dependencies can be unit tested directly, without rendering anything.

quiz.question: What's a well-known real-world framework built around MVC?
quiz.explanation: Rails is one of the most widely known frameworks explicitly structured around the Model-View-Controller pattern.
